title: The cycle (Judges 2:16–19)
hook: forget, suffer, cry out, be rescued, forget again: the book of Judges in one loop

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joshua's last speech at Shechem, and your line was choose this day. What did you choose for your house? Day seven hundred two.

Forget. Suffer. Cry out. Be rescued. Forget again. That is the book of Judges in one loop, and the book lays it out itself, near the start, before any of its famous stories begin. Joshua has died, and his whole generation with him. Then the text says it plainly: "there arose another generation after them, which knew not the LORD, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel." The people who carried stones up out of the river are gone. The next generation, it seems, never heard the answer to the question the stones were built to raise. What follows is a loop, and today's word names the people God keeps sending into it.

The word is judge. In English it sounds like a courtroom: a robe, a bench, a gavel. Listen to how the book introduces them, in the King James Bible: "Nevertheless the LORD raised up judges, which delivered them out of the hand of those that spoiled them." Delivered. These judges are rescuers first: leaders raised up in a crisis. Some lead in battle. Some settle disputes. The Hebrew word is shofet. Now the loop. The people turn to other gods. They're handed over to raiders. They groan under it, and here the text says something tender: "it repented the LORD because of their groanings by reason of them that oppressed them and vexed them." God is moved by their groaning. A judge is raised up, and while that judge lives, there's rest. Then verse nineteen: "when the judge was dead, that they returned, and corrupted themselves more than their fathers." More than their fathers. It isn't a circle. It's a spiral, and it's heading down. By the very last verse of the book, the narrator puts it in one line: "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes." Readers find two things in this loop at once. One is a warning: the first step is forgetting, and forgetting makes no noise. In chapter two, a generation grows up without the story first, and only then do the other gods follow. The other is mercy. Again and again, when they cry out, someone is sent. What runs short is remembering.

Here's the practice: notice one loop in your life. Settle, and breathe. Loops are often quiet: the same argument, the same late-night scrolling, the same promise on Monday that's gone by Thursday. Let one come to mind. Trace it slowly. Where does it start? What's the forgetting part, the moment you stop paying attention? Where's the groaning? What usually rescues you, for a while? Don't fix it now. Just see the whole loop once, clearly, without beating yourself up. If you pray, you can name it to God, the way Israel groaned. If you don't, simply hold it in view and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Judge. In the book of Judges, a shofet: someone raised up in a crisis to deliver and set things right. Not a robe and a gavel.
Your line: break the cycle. Today, find the forgetting point in your loop, and put one small reminder right there, where it starts. Day seven hundred two.

howItsDone: Some Christians read Judges 2 as the key to the whole book, and some preachers use its cycle to speak about patterns of forgetting God and returning.

fork.setup: you're living in the days of the judges. a judge has rescued your people, and now that judge has died. what does the text say happens next?
options: they go back to the old ways, worse than before.
they choose a king right away.
fork.reveal: "when the judge was dead... they returned, and corrupted themselves more than their fathers." the loop starts again, lower down.

original.note: Hebrew: judge. Judges 2:16 says the LORD raised up shoftim, judges, which delivered them.

trapdoor: what you thought: a judge sits in a courtroom.
what it means: in Judges, a judge is a deliverer raised up when the people cry out, inside a loop that keeps coming back.
what a scholar hears: shofet, and Judges 2:11–19 as the pattern for the whole book, a spiral that ends at 21:25: no king, every man right in his own eyes.

notes: Shofet glossed as 'someone who sets things right, by a verdict or by a rescue'; the book's judges include both military deliverers and Deborah, who 'judged' disputes (4:4–5). Confirm the gloss.
'A generation grows up without the story first, and only then do the other gods follow' reads the order of 2:10–12 (2:12: they forsook the LORD). Confirm it is fair.
'Their children's children, it seems, never heard the answer' links back to Joshua 4:6 (day 699); an interpretive bridge, hedged with 'it seems'.
Shoftim as the Hebrew name of the book. Confirm the original's pointing and pronunciation.

Editor (y3 audit): 'children's children' changed to 'the next generation' (2:10 says another generation); the shofet gloss and the claim about the book's Hebrew name cut (not in the cited text); 'the book never runs out of rescuers' softened, since its last chapters have no judge.
